# Project Guidelines

## Language & Runtime

- PowerShell 7.4+ (LTS) is required. Entry-point and dot-sourced scripts carry `#Requires -Version 7.4`; the only exception is `Setup-Prerequisites.ps1`, which must run on Windows PowerShell 5.1 so it can tell users how to install PowerShell 7.
- Modern syntax (ternary operator, null-coalescing, `&&`/`||`, `clean` blocks) is allowed and preferred where it improves readability. Don't rewrite working code just to modernize it.
- `[System.Security.Cryptography.*]` .NET 8 classes are available (including `AesGcm`).

## Architecture

- **Single-checkout model**: Only one copy of this repository is used per PowerShell session. The credential cache (`$global:__IntuneCachedMasterKey`, `$global:__IntuneCachedTenantSecrets`) is intentionally session-global so that consecutive `Deploy-ToIntune.ps1` runs don't re-prompt for the master password. Do not suggest scoping the cache per config file path — this is a deliberate design trade-off documented in TenantConfig.ps1 and README.md.
- **Cache invalidation is by design minimal**: The cached master key and tenant secrets are not revalidated against `intune-tenants.json` on each use. Out-of-band config changes (manual file edits, git pulls) require `Clear-IntuneTenantCache` or a new PowerShell session. Client-secret rotation uses the documented remove+re-add flow (`Remove-IntuneTenant` then `Add-IntuneTenant`), which clears the relevant cache entries. Do not suggest adding cache-invalidation logic or config-file change detection.
- `TenantConfig.ps1` is dot-sourced by `Deploy-ToIntune.ps1` — `$script:` scoped variables would not persist across runs, which is why `$global:` is used for caching.
- `AppConfig.ps1` defines all application metadata as a hashtable. New apps are added there.
- **App families**: `Get-AppFamilyCatalog` / `Resolve-AppFamily` / `Get-AppFamilyNamePattern` / `Get-AppFamilyBaseName` / `Get-IntuneAppVersion` in `SharedFunctions.ps1` are the one way to map an Intune app to its AppConfig family and version. **Membership requires the naming convention**: the display name must match `<base> <version>[ suffix]` as derived from the `DisplayNameTemplate` (regex from `Get-AppFamilyNamePattern`), not merely start with the base name — otherwise "Google Chrome Remote Desktop 2.0" would be a Chrome version and, since membership feeds the retention cleanup, a deletion candidate. Apps that share a base name but don't follow the convention (a bare "Google Chrome", a hand-deployed variant with a different suffix) are unmanaged: never superseded, never deleted; renaming them to the template brings them under management. Deploy-ToIntune.ps1 (existing-version search and dependency lookup) and the inventory/cleanup tooling all use this classifier.
- **`IntuneSession.ps1`** holds the tenant session bootstrap (`Resolve-IntuneTenantCredential`, `Install-RequiredModules`, `Connect-IntuneTenantSession`) shared by every script that talks to a tenant; it dot-sources `AuthenticationManager.ps1` and `TenantConfig.ps1`. Kept out of `SharedFunctions.ps1` so the packaging script never loads credentials or Graph auth. Tenant-facing scripts wrap everything after `Connect-IntuneTenantSession` in `try { } finally { Disconnect-IntuneSession -Force }` so the privileged Graph session is dropped on every exit path (`exit` inside `try` runs `finally` in pwsh).
- **Cleanup**: apps are deleted in exactly one place, `Invoke-IntuneAppCleanup` (`IntuneCleanup.ps1`, with `Write-AppCleanupLog`), driven by two callers: `Remove-OldIntuneAppVersions.ps1` (interactive, tenant-wide, `SupportsShouldProcess` with `ConfirmImpact High` — its ShouldProcess is the executor's `-Decision` hook) and `Deploy-ToIntune.ps1` (unattended, per deployed family, only with a deployment plan whose tenant opted in, `-NoRetention` to skip). Both evaluate the tenant live through the same read path as the inventory (`Read-IntuneAppInventory` in `IntuneInventory.ps1` → `Get-AppInventoryAnalysis`) and execute the pure planner `Get-AppCleanupPlan` (`AppCleanup.ps1`): delete candidates of in-plan families, oldest first; everything else is skipped with a reason and no parameter can widen that (tenant opt-in via a tenant-level `Retention` block is mandatory).
- **Deploy and the graph limit**: `Deploy-ToIntune.ps1` reads the families it deploys once (`Read-IntuneAppInventory -OnlyFamilies`) and hands each family's records to `Publish-App -ExistingApps` (no per-app tenant listing). Before uploading, `Test-SupersedenceHeadroom` (pure, `AppInventory.ps1`) checks that the version to be superseded does not already sit in a full 11-node graph — otherwise the app fails before the upload with a pointer to the cleanup. A supersedence that fails after the upload is a deployment failure (the app is left without assignments, never assigned unlinked). Intune returns 400 on `DELETE mobileApps/{id}` while the app is part of a supersedence relationship, so `Remove-InteropAppRelationships` runs first. The per-relationship `DELETE mobileApps/{id}/relationships/{id}` that the Graph reference documents is **not implemented by the service** (400 "No OData route exists … with http verb DELETE"); removal is `updateRelationships` on the relationship's *owner* — the superseding app (relationship ids are `{sourceId}_{targetId}`) — re-submitting only its remaining child-direction set (`ConvertTo-InteropRelationshipBody`; parent-direction entries belong to the other app and are never re-submitted, so the rest of the chain stays untouched). It reads the relationships fresh **after** the confirmation prompt (which may sit open for a long time), refuses to touch an app that has become a dependency target, and reports partial removals (`Removed` of `Total` + `Error`) so the log records an app left unlinked. Wrappers that write surface Graph's error body via `Get-InteropErrorMessage` — a bare "BadRequest" is not an acceptable error. Decisions are logged to `inventory/<Tenant>-cleanup-<yyyyMMdd-HHmmss>.json`, never overwritten. A saved inventory JSON is documentation, never the authority for a delete.
- **Inventory**: `Get-IntuneAppInventory.ps1` is read-only. It fetches through `IntuneInterop.ps1` (`Get-InteropWin32App`, `Get-InteropAppAssignmentDetail`, `Get-InteropAppRelationship`, and one tenant-wide `Get-InteropAppInstallSummaryReport` — the Intune reporting actions under `deviceManagement/reports/*` are the supported source for install counts; the per-app `mobileApps/{id}/installSummary`, `deviceStatuses` and `userStatuses` resources are retired) and hands raw objects to the pure `AppInventory.ps1` (`ConvertTo-AppInventoryRecord` → `Get-AppInventoryAnalysis` → `Format-AppInventoryMarkdown`), which is what the tests drive with synthetic data. Reports go to `inventory/` (git-ignored). Analysis rules worth knowing: supersedence graphs are connected components over supersedence edges (warn at 9 of Intune's 11 nodes); families with version-comparison detection (`greaterThanOrEqual`, script rules) are marked *inflating* because older versions keep detecting as installed — a reporting caveat for their install counts only. **A superseded version keeping its 'available' assignment is normal and required** (the Company Portal hides it behind the newest version, and the assignment keeps supersedence/auto-update working) — never flag or remove that; what does appear as a separate Company Portal app is an older version assigned *available* that nothing supersedes (`OlderVersionUnlinked`, e.g. after a chain split at the graph limit; required-only assignments are not visible in the portal); near-miss names (share a base name, break the convention) get a `NamingConventionMismatch` anomaly with a rename suggestion.
- **Version retention**: policy lives in `TenantDeployments.json` (`Retention` block per tenant, overridable per app; defaults keep newest 3 + everything younger than 10 weeks; `KeepNewest` floor is 2 because Intune irrevocably drops Company Portal auto-update tracking when a superseded app's assignment disappears). `Get-TenantRetentionPolicy` resolves it; a tenant-level block is the opt-in for automated cleanup. `AppRetention.ps1` (`Get-AppRetentionPlan`, `Select-AppRetentionDeleteCandidates`) is the pure evaluator - no Graph, no file access - shared by the inventory report and the cleanup. Duplicate version numbers are `Review`, never auto-deleted; unparseable versions, unknown creation dates and dependency targets are always kept. A failed relationship read is recorded as `RelationshipsUnavailable` (never as an empty set) and the analysis downgrades that app's `Delete` to `Review` - it might be a dependency target the inventory cannot see.
- **`IntuneInterop.ps1` is the Intune API layer**: every Intune call is a native Microsoft Graph request (`Invoke-MgGraphRequest` against `beta`, `-OutputType PSObject`) riding the `Connect-MgGraph` session from `AuthenticationManager.ps1`. Everything else uses the `*-Interop*` wrapper functions, which take plain domain values and return Graph-schema shaped hashtables. Key mechanics: `Get-InteropWin32App` uses a paged `isof` list + per-ID GET (the list endpoint validates `$select` against the base `mobileApp` type, so derived properties can't be selected there); `updateRelationships` REPLACES an app's full relationship set, so the supersedence/dependency wrappers read and re-submit the other relationship type; `Publish-InteropWin32App` does create app → content version → extract the pre-encrypted payload from the `.intunewin` → chunked Azure Storage upload with SAS renewal → commit with `fileEncryptionInfo` from Detection.xml → PATCH `committedContentVersion`.
- **The third-party `IntuneWin32App` module is no longer used** (removed in 3.2.0 after being isolated in #8 and replaced natively in #9). Do not reintroduce it — the AST-based boundary check in `pwsh-validate.yml` remains as a tripwire and fails CI on any `*-IntuneWin32App*` cmdlet call or assignment to its legacy auth globals outside `IntuneInterop.ps1`.

## Cryptography Design Decisions

- **AES-256-GCM** (AEAD) protects client secrets in `intune-tenants.json`. Blob layout (base64): salt (16 bytes) + nonce (12 bytes) + tag (16 bytes) + ciphertext. The GCM tag authenticates the ciphertext, so a wrong password or tampering is detected deterministically at decrypt time. The threat model remains casual exposure (accidental commits, screen visibility), not active attackers with filesystem write access.
- **PBKDF2 with 600,000 iterations and SHA-256** for key derivation — meets current OWASP recommendations. Uses the static `[Rfc2898DeriveBytes]::Pbkdf2()` method.
- **Config format version 3 is the only supported format.** `intune-tenants.json` carries a top-level `"version": 3`. Older (v2.x, AES-CBC) files are rejected with instructions to re-add tenants — there is intentionally no migration or legacy-decrypt path. Do not suggest adding backward compatibility for pre-3.0 configs.
- `Unprotect-Secret` catches `CryptographicException` and `FormatException` (malformed base64) and returns `$null` on wrong password or tampered data; unexpected exceptions propagate.

## Code Patterns

- `AutoUpdate` in `AppConfig.ps1` controls whether the Intune assignment setting "If superseded app(s) have been installed by the user from Company Portal, require superseding app to be installed" is enabled. It does **not** control `DetectionOperator` — those are independent properties. `DetectionOperator` determines version comparison logic (`greaterThanOrEqual`, `equal`, `ProductCodeOnly`, `ScriptOnly`) and is set explicitly per app.
- Use `SecureString` + `SecureStringToBSTR` for user-facing password input; internal crypto helpers accept plain strings (suppressed via `PSScriptAnalyzer` attributes at file level).
- Always dispose `IDisposable` crypto objects (`AesGcm`, `RandomNumberGenerator`) in `try/finally` blocks.
- Always free BSTR pointers with `ZeroFreeBSTR` in `finally` blocks.
- `Read-TenantConfig` throws on parse/schema errors rather than returning empty config (prevents silent data loss on corrupt JSON).

## Build & Test

- Syntax validation: `[System.Management.Automation.Language.Parser]::ParseFile()` — used in CI via `.github/workflows/pwsh-validate.yml`
- Pester test suite in `tests/` (Pester v5+ syntax; run: `Invoke-Pester -Path tests`). Fully offline — no Graph connection or IntuneWin32App module needed. CI runs it on `windows-latest` with Pester pinned (6.0.1 — bump the pin in `pwsh-validate.yml` deliberately), excluding tag `LocalOnly` (tests that need real installer binaries from `packages/`, which are not in git).
- Test files copy the scripts under test to `$TestDrive` before dot-sourcing, so `$PSScriptRoot`-derived paths (`intune-tenants.json`, `AppVersions.json`, detection scripts) stay sandboxed — keep that pattern when adding tests.
- `tests/AppInventory.Tests.ps1` drives the inventory analysis with a synthetic tenant that reproduces the real findings (a family at the graph limit, `>=`-detected family with older versions still assigned, an auto-update gap, a near-miss name, a protected dependency target, a duplicate version). Extend that fixture when adding analysis rules.
- `tests/AppConfig.Tests.ps1` is the golden guard for app-config generation: it pins the detection/requirement rule shapes and command lines that refactors (issue #8 interop isolation, #9 native Graph migration) must preserve. If it fails after an intentional contract change, update the assertions deliberately.
